## Why the method exists

General Motors invests on a scale Westinghouse never reaches, at the same
market value and the same capital stock. Each of Grunfeld's ten firms has a
character of its own, and so does each of the 49 states whose house prices
run through this book. Call that character $\alpha_i$, the **unit effect**:
everything about unit *i* that does not change over the sample and is not in
the regression. In an earnings equation it is unobserved ability; in a
production function it is managerial skill [@baltagi2021, p. 15].

One pooled regression puts $\alpha_i$ in the error, and that does two kinds
of damage. The errors of one unit are then correlated across every pair of
years by the same amount, so the pooled standard errors are wrong
[@moulton1986; @baltagi2021, pp. 24, 54]. And if $\alpha_i$ moves with the
regressors, as ability moves with schooling, the pooled slope is biased: an
omitted-variable bias, since the unit dummies that belong in the equation
were left out [@baltagi2021, p. 18].

**Fixed effects** treat $\alpha_i$ as a parameter, one per unit, and either
estimate it with a dummy or wipe it out by taking each unit's data in
deviation from its own mean. The price is that only within-unit variation is
left: $N - 1$ degrees of freedom are gone, and any regressor that does not
change over time, sex, schooling, a state's land area, is wiped out with the
effect [@baltagi2021, p. 17]. **Random effects** treat $\alpha_i$ as a draw,
$\alpha_i \sim \mathrm{IID}(0, \sigma^2_\alpha)$, independent of the
regressors. The price is that independence assumption; the gain is
efficiency, because between-unit variation is used too, and a coefficient on
the time-invariant regressors [@baltagi2021, p. 24]. Mundlak put the choice
sharply: random effects assume every regressor is uncorrelated with
$\alpha_i$, fixed effects allow every one to be correlated, "an 'all' or
'nothing' choice" [@baltagi2021, p. 28]. The rest of this note is about how
to tell whether $\alpha_i$ is there at all, and then which of the two
stories fits.

## 1. One error, two components

One regression for all units assumes two things: the same slopes for every
unit, and an error whose only structure is the unit effect. Write the model
as

$$
y_{it} = \beta' x_{it} + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad
u_{it} = \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it},
$$

with $\varepsilon_{it} \sim \mathrm{IID}(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon)$, the
**one-way error component model** [@baltagi2021, eqs. 2.1–2.2, p. 15]. The
**two-way** model adds a time effect, $u_{it} = \alpha_i + \delta_t +
\varepsilon_{it}$, a strike year or an oil shock that hits every unit in that
year [@baltagi2021, eq. 3.1, p. 47]; Baltagi writes it $\lambda_t$. The
same-slopes assumption is **poolability**, and its tests, Chow's F,
Roy–Zellner and Swamy's random coefficients, are in [the error
note](theory-panel-error.qmd); this note takes the slopes as common and asks
what $\alpha_i$ is.

Under random effects the composite error has covariance

$$
\Omega = \sigma^2_\alpha (I_N \otimes J_T) + \sigma^2_\varepsilon I_{NT},
$$

where $J_T$ is a $T \times T$ matrix of ones [@baltagi2021, eq. 2.17, p.
24]. Two errors of the same unit, any two years apart, are correlated by
$\rho = \sigma^2_\alpha / (\sigma^2_\alpha + \sigma^2_\varepsilon)$, however
far apart the years; errors of different units are uncorrelated
[@baltagi2021, p. 24]. That constant $\rho$ is the signature of a unit
effect, and the serial-correlation tests of the error note are built to
tell it from an autoregressive error, whose correlation dies out with the
distance between years.

## 2. Within, between and GLS

Two projection matrices do all the work. $P = I_N \otimes \bar J_T$, with
$\bar J_T = J_T / T$, replaces every observation by its unit mean; $Q =
I_{NT} - P$ takes deviations from the unit mean. They are symmetric,
idempotent, orthogonal, and sum to the identity [@baltagi2021, p. 16;
@croissant2019, p. 25]. The **within** estimator regresses $Qy$ on $QX$,

$$
\hat\beta_W = (X'QX)^{-1} X'Qy,
$$

and $Q$ wipes out $\alpha_i$ with the unit means [@baltagi2021, eq. 2.7, p.
17]. The **between** estimator regresses the unit means on each other,
$\hat\beta_B = (X'PX)^{-1} X'Py$, and uses only the variation across units
[@baltagi2021, eq. 2.25, p. 26]. Pooled OLS weights the two sources of
variation equally; GLS weights them by the inverse of their variances
[@baltagi2021, pp. 26–27]. With $\phi^2 = \sigma^2_\varepsilon /
\sigma^2_1$ and $\sigma^2_1 = T\sigma^2_\alpha + \sigma^2_\varepsilon$,

$$
\hat\beta_{GLS} = W_1 \hat\beta_W + W_2 \hat\beta_B, \qquad
W_1 = [X'QX + \phi^2 X'PX]^{-1} X'QX, \quad W_2 = I - W_1,
$$

a matrix-weighted average of within and between [@baltagi2021, eq. 2.31,
pp. 26–27; @croissant2019, sec. 2.4.1, p. 39]. Two limits say what the
estimator is doing. If $\sigma^2_\alpha = 0$ then $\phi^2 = 1$ and GLS is
OLS. If $T \to \infty$ then $\phi^2 \to 0$ and GLS is within [@baltagi2021,
p. 27; @pesaran2015, p. 653]: with enough years per unit the two stories
give the same slope, and the fixed-or-random question only bites when *T* is
short.

In practice GLS is OLS on **quasi-demeaned** data. Premultiplying by
$\Omega^{-1/2}$ turns $y_{it}$ into $y_{it} - \theta \bar y_{i\cdot}$ with

$$
\theta = 1 - \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon}{\sigma_1}
  = 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + T\sigma^2_\alpha / \sigma^2_\varepsilon}},
$$

the fraction of the unit mean that is removed [@baltagi2021, eq. 2.20, p.
25; @croissant2019, p. 35]. $\theta = 0$ is pooled OLS, $\theta = 1$ is
within, and `plm::ercomp` prints it: 0.86 on Grunfeld, which is why every
feasible GLS fit there sits next to the within fit [@baltagi2021, p. 31].

The variance components have to be estimated first, and the menu in
`random.method` is a menu of residuals. Wallace–Hussain use pooled OLS
residuals in the two quadratic forms $u'Pu/N$ and $u'Qu/N(T-1)$; Amemiya
uses the within residuals instead, which gives the same asymptotic
distribution as knowing the true disturbances [@baltagi2021, eqs. 2.21–2.23,
p. 25]; Swamy–Arora take $\hat\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ from the within
regression's mean square and $\hat\sigma^2_1$ from the between regression's
[@swamy1972; @baltagi2021, eqs. 2.24 and 2.27, pp. 25–26]; Nerlove estimates
$\sigma^2_\alpha$ as the sample variance of the estimated dummies
[@baltagi2021, p. 27; @croissant2019, pp. 36–37]. All but Nerlove recover
$\sigma^2_\alpha = (\sigma^2_1 - \sigma^2_\varepsilon)/T$ by subtraction, and
nothing stops the difference from being negative. In the one-way model the
fix is to set it to zero, which happens only when the true variance is near
zero, when OLS is fine anyway, so "replacing negative $\sigma^2_\mu$ by zero
is not a sin after all" [@baltagi2021, p. 27]. In the two-way model Baltagi's
Monte Carlo says the opposite: a negative estimate cannot be told from a
misspecified model, and "the researcher should not label the problem of
negative variance estimates 'not serious'" [@baltagi1981; @baltagi2021, p.
56].

The two-way model has four distinct roots of $\Omega$ and three variance
components, so GLS is a matrix-weighted average of three estimators: within,
between units $\hat\beta_B$ and between periods $\hat\beta_C$ [@baltagi2021,
eqs. 3.13 and 3.24, pp. 51–53], and Swamy–Arora's recipe needs three
regressions [@baltagi2021, eqs. 3.19–3.21, p. 52]. The time variance
component is estimated from $T - 1$ period means, so on a panel with 20
years it is the one most likely to come back negative. That is what happens
to Grunfeld under Swamy–Arora and Wallace–Hussain [@baltagi2021, p. 99], and
it is why the two-way Hausman statistic of section 5 depends on the method.

## 3. Is there an effect at all

The **Breusch–Pagan** test asks whether pooled OLS residuals from one unit
resemble each other more than chance allows. It is a Lagrange multiplier
test: a score test that needs only the restricted model, here pooled OLS,
and under normality the score for $\sigma^2_\alpha$ is a function of the
ratio of the summed squared unit totals to the summed squared residuals
[@breusch1980; @baltagi2021, eqs. 4.17–4.22, pp. 81–82]. For
$H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0$,

$$
LM_1 = \frac{NT}{2(T-1)}
  \left[ \frac{\hat u'(I_N \otimes J_T)\hat u}{\hat u'\hat u} - 1 \right]^2
  \;\sim\; \chi^2_1 ,
$$

and the test of $\sigma^2_\delta = 0$ swaps $I_N \otimes J_T$ for $J_N
\otimes I_T$ and $T - 1$ for $N - 1$; the two-way test of both is their sum,
$\chi^2_2$ [@baltagi2021, eqs. 4.22–4.24, p. 82].

The alternative of a two-sided test is "the variance is not zero", and a
variance cannot be negative. **Honda** takes the signed square root,

$$
A = \sqrt{\frac{NT}{2(T-1)}}
  \left[ \frac{\hat u'(I_N \otimes J_T)\hat u}{\hat u'\hat u} - 1 \right]
  \;\sim\; N(0, 1),
$$

and rejects only for large positive values; it is uniformly most powerful
for the one-sided alternative and robust to non-normality [@honda1985;
@baltagi2021, eq. 4.25, p. 83]. The sign matters. On Grunfeld the time-effect
statistic is $B = -2.540$: the one-sided test does not reject, but $B^2 =
6.454$ is above the $\chi^2_1$ critical value 3.841 and the two-sided test
does. The one-sided test is right; "these data clearly support the use of
the one-sided test in empirical applications" [@baltagi2021, p. 87].

For both effects at once Honda offers the "handy" $(A + B)/\sqrt 2$, which
is $N(0, 1)$ under the null [@baltagi2021, p. 83]. **King–Wu** replace the
equal weights by the locally mean most powerful ones,

$$
KW = \sqrt{\frac{T-1}{N+T-2}}\, A + \sqrt{\frac{N-1}{N+T-2}}\, B ,
$$

also $N(0, 1)$ [@king1997; @baltagi1992; @baltagi2021, eq. 4.30, p. 84].
Both can be dragged down by a negative piece. **Gourieroux, Holly and
Monfort** drop a negative piece instead of adding it:

$$
\chi^2_m =
\begin{cases}
A^2 + B^2 & A > 0,\ B > 0 \\
A^2       & A > 0,\ B \le 0 \\
B^2       & A \le 0,\ B > 0 \\
0         & A \le 0,\ B \le 0 ,
\end{cases}
\qquad
\chi^2_m \sim \tfrac14 \chi^2(0) + \tfrac12 \chi^2(1) + \tfrac14 \chi^2(2),
$$

a **mixed chi-square** whose weights come from *A* and *B* being
asymptotically independent; it "is immune to the possible negative values
of A and B" [@gourieroux1982; @baltagi1992; @baltagi2021, eq. 4.33, p. 84].
In Baltagi, Chang and Li's Monte Carlo, Breusch–Pagan, Honda and King–Wu all
under-size the joint test when a piece is negative, while GHM and the F test
hold their size [@baltagi2021, p. 86]. `plm::plmtest(type = "ghm")` exists
for `effect = "twoways"` only, which is where it is needed.

Two refinements are not implemented. Moulton and Randolph showed that the
$N(0, 1)$ approximation for Honda's statistic "can be poor even in large
samples ... when the number of regressors is large or the intra-class
correlation of some of the regressors is high", and proposed the
**standardized LM** test, Honda's statistic centred and scaled by the exact
mean and variance of the quadratic form,
$SLM = (d - E(d))/\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(d)}$ with
$d = \hat u' D \hat u / \hat u'\hat u$ [@moulton1989; @honda1991;
@baltagi2021, eqs. 4.26–4.28, p. 83]. Spatially smooth regressors have a
high intra-class correlation, so this is the case of this book. And testing
$\sigma^2_\alpha = 0$ with Honda's statistic "implicitly assumes that the
time-specific effects do not exist", which "may lead to incorrect decisions
especially when the variance of the time effects (assumed to be zero) is
large". The **conditional LM** tests of Baltagi, Chang and Li test one
variance allowing the other to be positive, from one-way GLS residuals
[@baltagi1992; @baltagi2021, eqs. 4.34 and 4.36, p. 85]; the Monte Carlo
verdict is that "one should not ignore the possibility that $\sigma^2_\lambda
> 0$ when testing $\sigma^2_\mu = 0$", and that over-specifying the model as
two-way costs little [@baltagi2021, p. 86]. `plmtest(effect = "twoways")`
tests both variances jointly; it is not this conditional test.

The oldest test is an **F** on the unit dummies: pooled OLS is the
restricted model, within the unrestricted, and

$$
F = \frac{(RRSS - URSS)/(N-1)}{URSS/(NT - N - K)}
  \;\sim\; F_{N-1,\, N(T-1)-K}
$$

[@baltagi2021, eq. 2.12, p. 18; eq. 4.38, p. 85]. In the two-way model
there are three such tests: both sets of dummies against pooled OLS, unit
dummies given time dummies, and time dummies given unit dummies, each with
the two-way within fit as the unrestricted model [@baltagi2021, eqs.
3.8–3.9, p. 49]. These conditional F tests are exact in finite samples under
normality, "perform reasonably well when compared to the LR and LM tests,
for both the one-way and two-way models and are recommended" [@baltagi2021,
p. 87]; they are the three rows of Baltagi's Table 4.3 [@baltagi2021, p.
89], and `plm::pFtest` on two nested within fits is the conditional pair.

## 4. Fixed or random: the Hausman contrast

Everything above finds an effect; nothing says whether it is correlated
with the regressors. The random-effects GLS estimator is efficient when
$E(u_{it} \mid X_{it}) = 0$ and inconsistent otherwise; the within estimator
is consistent either way, because $Q$ removed $\alpha_i$ before the
regression. **Hausman's** idea is to compare them: if both are consistent
they should agree, and the covariance of an efficient estimator with its
difference from any other consistent estimator is zero, so the variance of
the difference is the difference of the variances [@hausman1978;
@baltagi2021, pp. 89–90; @pesaran2015, eq. 26.52, p. 660]. With $\hat q_1 =
\hat\beta_{GLS} - \hat\beta_W$,

$$
\mathrm{var}(\hat q_1)
  = \mathrm{var}(\hat\beta_W) - \mathrm{var}(\hat\beta_{GLS}),
\qquad
m_1 = \hat q_1' [\mathrm{var}(\hat q_1)]^{-1} \hat q_1 \;\sim\; \chi^2_K
$$

[@baltagi2021, eqs. 4.40–4.41, p. 90]. The same test is a Wald test in an
**augmented regression**: quasi-demean $y$ and $X$ as GLS does, add the
within-demeaned regressors $\tilde X = QX$, and test their coefficient,

$$
y^* = X^*\beta + \tilde X \gamma + w, \qquad H_0: \gamma = 0
$$

[@baltagi2021, eq. 4.42, p. 90]. OLS on this regression returns
$\hat\beta = \hat\beta_B$ and $\hat\gamma = \hat\beta_W - \hat\beta_B$, with
$\mathrm{var}(\hat\gamma) = \mathrm{var}(\hat\beta_W) +
\mathrm{var}(\hat\beta_B)$, a sum, since the two use orthogonal pieces of
the data [@baltagi2021, eqs. 4.46–4.48, pp. 90–91]. Hausman and Taylor
proved that the three contrasts, GLS against within, GLS against between,
and within against between, give numerically identical statistics
[@hausman1981; @baltagi2021, p. 91]; `phtest(method = "chisq")` is $m_1$
and `method = "aux"` is the augmented regression. On Grunfeld they are 2.33
and 2.13, the difference being only which $\hat\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ enters
the variance [@baltagi2021, p. 95].

The augmented regression is also how the test is made robust. Under
heteroskedasticity or serial correlation neither estimator is efficient, so
the variance of the contrast is no longer a difference of variances and
$m_1$ is wrong. **Arellano** writes the contrast as a regression on forward
orthogonal deviations stacked over unit means, with $\hat\gamma =
\hat\beta_B - \hat\beta_W$, and tests $\gamma = 0$ with White's robust
covariance [@arellano1993; @baltagi2021, eq. 4.49, pp. 91–92]; "a simpler
robust Hausman test can be obtained by testing for $\gamma = 0$ from the
artificial regression (4.42) using the robust variance-covariance option"
[@baltagi2021, p. 92; @croissant2019, sec. 5.1.3.1, p. 125], which is
`phtest(method = "aux", vcov = plm::vcovHC)`. On Grunfeld Baltagi's robust
F(2, 195) is 1.58, p 0.208 [@baltagi2021, p. 95]; with ten clusters the
Arellano covariance is itself noisy, and the step reports what plm gives.

**Mundlak's** reading says what is being tested. Let the unit effect be a
linear function of the unit means of the regressors,

$$
\alpha_i = \pi' \bar x_{i\cdot} + w_i, \qquad
w_i \sim \mathrm{IID}(0, \sigma^2_w).
$$

Substituting it in gives $y = X\beta + PX\pi + (\alpha + \varepsilon)$, an
error-components model with the unit means as extra regressors, and GLS on
it returns $\hat\beta = \hat\beta_W$ and $\hat\pi = \hat\beta_B -
\hat\beta_W$: once the correlation is modelled, the efficient estimator is
within, and the random-effects estimator is biased because it ignores $\pi$
[@mundlak1978; @baltagi2021, eqs. 7.33–7.38, pp. 170–171; @croissant2019,
sec. 4.2.1, pp. 89–90]. Hausman's test is the test of $\pi = 0$. It is
worth saying what a rejection does not show. "Rejecting the null of the
Hausman test implies that the RE estimator is not consistent. This does not
necessarily mean that the FE restrictions are satisfied" [@baltagi2021, p.
93]. Chamberlain's restrictions, that the reduced-form regression of each
year's $y$ on every year's $x$ has the structure $\Pi = (I_T \otimes
\beta') + \iota_T \lambda'$, are testable; Angrist and Newey showed that the
minimum chi-square statistic is a sum over periods of degrees of freedom
times the $R^2$ from regressing that period's within residuals on all leads
and lags of the regressors [@chamberlain1982; @angrist1991; @baltagi2021,
eqs. 4.50–4.53, pp. 92–93; @croissant2019, sec. 4.2.3, pp. 90–93]. Both need
*N* large against $T K$, which is why `plm::piest` fails on ten firms and
runs on 595 workers. One more caution: using the Hausman test to pick the
estimator and then testing $\beta$ distorts the size of the second test, and
Guggenberger's advice is fixed-effects inference without the pretest
[@baltagi2021, p. 94].

## 5. The two-way case

With a time effect as well, the contrast of two-way GLS with two-way within
is still a Hausman test, and the augmented regression still works with the
two-way transformations [@baltagi2021, p. 99]. What breaks is the
equivalence of section 4. There are now two between estimators, across
units $\hat\beta_C$ and across periods $\hat\beta_T$, and GLS is a weighted
combination of three; **Kang** showed that the test based on within minus
GLS is not equivalent to the one based on either between estimator minus
GLS, and listed five testable hypotheses [@kang1985; @baltagi2021, p. 99]:

1. $\alpha_i$ fixed, test $E(\delta_t \mid X) = 0$ from
   $\hat\beta_W - \hat\beta_T$;
2. $\alpha_i$ random, test the same from $\hat\beta_T - \hat\beta_{GLS}$;
3. $\delta_t$ fixed, test $E(\alpha_i \mid X) = 0$ from
   $\hat\beta_W - \hat\beta_C$;
4. $\delta_t$ random, test the same from $\hat\beta_C - \hat\beta_{GLS}$;
5. both fixed against both random, from $\hat\beta_{GLS} - \hat\beta_W$.

`plm::phtest(effect = "twoways")` is hypothesis 5 and nothing else. On
Grunfeld it rejects: Baltagi's 8.842 on $\chi^2_2$, p 0.012 [@baltagi2021,
pp. 99–100], computed with EViews' Wansbeek–Kapteyn variance components
because Swamy–Arora and Wallace–Hussain return a negative
$\hat\sigma^2_\delta$ there [@wansbeek1989; @baltagi2021, p. 99]. plm has no
Wansbeek–Kapteyn option and truncates the negative component to zero, so the
statistic it prints depends on `random.method`, and none of its values is
8.842. The reading does not change: every diagnostic of section 3 says there
is no time effect on Grunfeld, so "one should not employ a two-way random
effects model, but rather a one-way random individual effects model"
[@baltagi2021, p. 101].

## 6. Time-invariant regressors

A rejection sends the reader to fixed effects, and fixed effects cannot
estimate the return to schooling, because schooling does not change over
the seven years of the wage panel. **Hausman and Taylor** keep some of the
random-effects story. Split the regressors into $X = [X_1, X_2]$ and the
time-invariant ones into $Z = [Z_1, Z_2]$, where the "1" blocks are
uncorrelated with $\alpha_i$ and the "2" blocks are correlated with it but
not with $\varepsilon_{it}$:

$$
y_{it} = \beta' x_{it} + \gamma' z_i + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

[@hausman1981; @baltagi2021, eq. 7.40, p. 171; @pesaran2015, sec. 26.10, p.
665]. The within transformation sweeps $\alpha_i$ and $z_i$ together. The
HT estimator is instead 2SLS on the $\Omega^{-1/2}$-transformed model with
instruments the panel generates itself, $A_{HT} = [QX_1, QX_2, PX_1, Z_1]$:
deviations of every time-varying regressor, which are orthogonal to
$\alpha_i$ by construction, plus the unit means of the exogenous ones and
the exogenous time-invariant regressors [@baltagi2021, p. 171;
@croissant2019, sec. 6.3.2.3, p. 146]. $X_1$ is used twice, as means and as
deviations, so the **order condition** is $k_1 \ge g_2$: at least as many
exogenous time-varying regressors as endogenous time-invariant ones
[@baltagi2021, p. 171; @croissant2019, p. 146]. If $k_1 = g_2$ the slopes on
$X$ are the within slopes; if $k_1 > g_2$ the model is over-identified, HT is
more efficient than within, and a Hausman contrast of the two tests the
over-identifying restrictions, $\chi^2$ with $k_1 - g_2$ degrees of freedom
[@baltagi2021, eq. 7.46, p. 172]. On the wage panel Baltagi reads $\chi^2_3
= 5.26$ as not rejecting, with three degrees of freedom "since there are
three over-identifying conditions" [@baltagi2021, p. 175]; `plm::phtest`
reports the number of common coefficients instead, nine, and the step says
so.

Amemiya and MaCurdy add $X_1$ at every period as instruments, which needs
$X_1$ to be uncorrelated with $\alpha_i$ period by period and not only on
average [@amemiya1986; @baltagi2021, p. 173; @croissant2019, p. 147];
Breusch, Mizon and Schmidt add the deviations of $X_2$ at every period too
[@breusch1989; @baltagi2021, p. 173]. Each set nests the one before, so the
extra assumptions are testable by a Hausman contrast of the two fits
[@croissant2019, p. 147], and the Cornwell–Rupert replication is the book's
worked case: GLS puts the return to schooling at 10 %, HT at 13.8 %, and
the HT-versus-AM contrast does not reject [@cornwell1988; @baltagi1990;
@baltagi2021, pp. 174–176]. When $z_i$ is uncorrelated with $\alpha_i$ no
instrument is needed: regress the unit means of the within residuals on
$z_i$ [@pesaran2015, sec. 26.10.1, pp. 663–664].

## If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| Honda's statistic is negative | No effect of that kind; do not read the squared Breusch–Pagan value as a rejection [@baltagi2021, p. 87] |
| Both effects are in question | Read GHM or the conditional F tests, which hold their size when a piece is negative [@baltagi2021, pp. 86–87] |
| Regressors are many or spatially smooth | Honda's $N(0, 1)$ reference can be poor; the SLM correction is not implemented [@baltagi2021, p. 83] |
| An effect is found and Hausman does not reject | Random effects is admissible and more efficient; report it beside within [@baltagi2021, p. 90] |
| Hausman rejects | Random effects is inconsistent; fixed effects is not thereby validated, and the Chamberlain restrictions remain to be tested [@baltagi2021, p. 93] |
| Errors are heteroskedastic or serially correlated | The $\chi^2$ form is wrong; use the augmented regression with a robust covariance [@baltagi2021, p. 92] |
| *T* is long | GLS and within converge; the choice matters little [@baltagi2021, p. 27; @pesaran2015, p. 653] |
| The two-way time variance comes back negative | The two-way Hausman statistic depends on the variance method; check whether a time effect is there at all [@baltagi2021, pp. 56, 99–101] |
| A time-invariant regressor matters and is endogenous | Hausman–Taylor with $k_1 \ge g_2$; test the instruments against within [@baltagi2021, pp. 171–172] |

## Open

- **The standardized LM tests** of Moulton–Randolph and Honda, Baltagi's
  eq. 4.26, are not implemented: `plmtest` has no `type = "slm"`, and the
  "Standardized" rows of Baltagi's Table 4.2 cannot be reproduced
  [@baltagi2021, pp. 83, 88].
- **The conditional LM tests** of Baltagi, Chang and Li, eqs. 4.34 and
  4.36, are not implemented; `plmtest(effect = "twoways")` is the joint
  test [@baltagi2021, p. 85].
- **Kang's five hypotheses** have one implementation, hypothesis 5;
  `phtest(effect = "time")` compares one-way time fixed with one-way time
  random effects and is none of Baltagi's Table 4.6 [@baltagi2021, pp.
  99–100].
- **Wansbeek–Kapteyn variance components** are not a `random.method`, so
  Baltagi's two-way 8.842 is not reproduced [@baltagi2021, p. 99].
- **Chamberlain's and Angrist–Newey's tests** need $N \gg TK$ and fail on
  Grunfeld; the chapter runs them on the wage panel instead.

## Next

The unit effect is one kind of error structure. The others, unequal
variances and memory in $\varepsilon_{it}$, and the standard errors that
survive them, are in [the error of a panel
regression](theory-panel-error.qmd).
